alt: Paper 3 lasts 1 hour 15 minutes, is worth 50 marks and 21% of the A Level. Four compulsory questions rise in marks from a short answer (AO1) to two explanations, two arguments against a quotation, and a 26-mark essay testing AO1, AO2 and AO3.
caption: Four compulsory questions climb in marks to a 26-mark essay.

after: ## 5.1 Functionalism: value consensus, solidarity and role allocation
alt: In the family a child is judged by particularistic standards and has ascribed status; school acts as a bridge to wider society, where everyone is judged by universalistic standards and status is achieved. Below, Davis and Moore’s role allocation and Tumin’s criticism.
caption: School moves children from family standards to the universal standards of society.

after: ## 5.1 Marxism: ideological control and cultural reproduction
alt: School life mirrors work life: pupils accept teachers’ authority as workers accept managers’, pupils work for grades as workers work for wages, and grades reward perseverance and punctuality, producing an obedient workforce. Willis shows pupils can resist, though reproduction still happens.
caption: For Bowles and Gintis, school life mirrors work life under capitalism.

after: ## 5.1 New Right and social democratic views on education and the economy
alt: Social democrats such as Halsey support state action for equal opportunity and draw on human capital theory; Wolf questions the link to growth. The New Right, following Chubb and Moe, wants marketisation through choice and competition; Gewirtz, Ball and Bowe show choice favours middle-class parents.
caption: Social democrats want the state to equalise; the New Right wants markets to raise standards.

after: ## 5.2 Meritocracy, life chances and social mobility
alt: A schematic of the occupational structure growing more middle-class jobs over time, so absolute upward mobility rises, while relative mobility stays stable because middle-class children keep their head start. Below, Goldthorpe’s study, the 1958 and 1970 cohort comparison and the Great Gatsby curve.
caption: More upward movement does not mean fairer chances: relative mobility can stay the same.

after: ## 5.2 Meritocracy, life chances and social mobility
alt: A cycle: more people gain a qualification, employers ask for a higher one, each qualification is worth less, and people seek higher credentials, so qualification inflation continues.
caption: As credentials spread, employers raise the bar and each one is worth less.

after: ## 5.3 Knowledge, the curriculum and cultural reproduction
alt: Power, status, culture, economic demands and gender shape the content of the curriculum, which Apple argues is not neutral. Three forms of cultural reproduction follow: the ethnocentric curriculum (Coard), the gendered curriculum (Spender) and the hidden curriculum (Jackson).
caption: Curriculum content reflects power, and reproduces culture through ethnocentric, gendered and hidden forms.

after: ## 5.3 Knowledge, the curriculum and cultural reproduction
alt: Bourdieu’s three forms of cultural capital: embodied (manner, speech, tastes), objectified (books, art, instruments) and institutionalised (qualifications). A chain shows habitus learned at home meeting a curriculum that rewards middle-class cultural capital, so middle-class pupils start ahead.
caption: Schools turn middle-class home culture into qualifications.
